newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's economic recovery seen slowing next year.
newsitem.headline: Japan's economic recovery seen slowing next year.

text.p: Japan's economy, slowly picking up this year after nearly four years of negligible growth, is likely to see the pace of the recovery slow in the next fiscal year, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Thursday.
Some of the economists expect the economy to return to an era of almost zero growth in the year starting from April.
Japan plunged into an economic recession in 1991 following the collapse of the so-called "bubble economy" of inflated land and asset prices.
Economists at banks, securities firms and research institutions in Tokyo and London were polled on October 15-17 on the Japanese economy.

The average of the forecasts on economic growth made by 28 economists showed that real gross domestic product (GDP) would grow by 2.5 percent for fiscal 1996/97 ending March 31, 1997. Real GDP for 1997/98 was expected to grow 1.9 percent.
Forecasts for this business year ranged from 1.7 percent to 3.8 percent, while for next year they ranged from 0.7 percent to 3.7 percent.
GDP is the value of goods and services produced over a given period, and real GDP is adjusted for inflation.
The government has officially forecast that real GDP would grow by 2.5 percent in 1996/97.

A slowdown in public works spending, a powerful engine of recent economic growth, and a scheduled increase in Japan's sales tax to five percent from three percent next April were the main reasons given for the expected slower growth next fiscal year.

"Consumer spending has already been slowing since earlier this year, and it will further worsen when the consumption tax is increased next April," said Shunsuke Motani, chief economist at Sphynx Investment Research based in Tokyo.
Motani said the only factor which would support the economy in the next fiscal year was exports, especially to the United States.
Michinori Nishimura, economist at LTCB Research Institute, said he expected the planned rise in the sales tax to bring down overall GDP by 0.7 percentage point.

Economists said they did not expect the government to adopt a large-scale supplementary budget for 1996/97 to stimulate the economy, given a snowballing state budget deficit which has become one of the worst among major nations.

But some senior government officials say Japan plans to adopt an extra budget later this year, in which economists predict the government will set aside about 3.5 trillion yen ($31.2 billion) for public works projects.
"If that's the size of the supplementary budget, it would help only to prevent the economy from contracting," Motani said.

Economists also forecast that slow economic growth will keep price increases in Japan to a minimum. The average of their predictions showed that the consumer price index, a key measure of inflation, would grow by 0.3 percent in 1996/97 and 1.5 percent in 1997/98.

Similarly, the average of their forecasts for the unemployment rate, which rose to a historic high of 3.5 percent in May 1996, showed it would stay at a high level of 3.4 percent in 1996/97 and 3.3 percent in 1997/98.
Japanese companies, hard hit by a prolonged slump, have been cutting the size of their workforce. ($1=112 yen)
